newsitem.title: UK: Overseas funds steer clear of U.S. bonds.
newsitem.headline: Overseas funds steer clear of U.S. bonds.

text.p: Waiting for economic growth to slow down in the U.S. has become a tedious job and many investment fund managers in Britain have given up, preferring to buy European bonds instead of Treasuries.
Managers said on Friday that new data only reinforced their view that a U.S. interest rate rise was merely a matter of time and reducing long term exposure to the U.S. market was prudent.
"On a three-month horizon we would favour Europe over the U.S.," said Robert Thomas at AMP Asset Management.

Rabbani Wahhabi, managing director at GH Asset Management said, "We haven't really had much exposure to U.S. Treasuries over the last month or so. There may be technical bounces...but in order to have some momentum behind them we need to see slower data."
Slower data certainly did not materialise on Thursday.
Second quarter growth was revised to 4.8 percent from 4.2 percent amid lower inventories and higher final sales. July new home sales soared 7.9 percent.
The yield on the benchmark long bond shot up to 7.04 percent, its highest level in a month.
Analysts said there may be more trouble ahead with August data from the National Association of Purchasing Management and crucial August payroll data next Friday.
"Our view is that the labour market is getting tighter and tighter and will begin to show pressure on wages," said Andy Canning, director of North American fixed income at BZW.
"If the payroll data are continuing to show strength the labour market tightness will probably need to be readdressed by the Fed," added Wahhabi.
In the meantime, many funds were staying underweight on the U.S. market.

"We're slightly underweight on the U.S. on a global basis and favour Europe," Canning said. "Even if there aren't any more rate cuts there certainly won't be any increases this year and probably not in the first half of next year either."

He said BZW which has about $400 million invested in its largest bond fund, was currently running a 33 percent weighting on Treasuries compared with 40 percent for the dollar bloc. The dollar bloc includes Australia and Canada.

Thomas at AMP said he would favour European high yielders over the U.S. Worries over several 1997 European budgets, to be presented in the weeks ahead, plus concerns over European Economic and Monetary Union would provide a chance to stock up.
"Until those issues are resolved it's going to be a bumpy ride and opportunities will exist to increase exposure to the high yielding markets and we would look to do so," he said.
Wahhabi at GH has been maintaing cash for its U.S. allocations, likes Britain for its reasonable growth and low inflation prospects and is neutral in Japan.
But fund managers said they would move back into the U.S. market once yields pushed up near the top of their 6-3/4 to 7-1/4 percent trading range.
"We'd probably looking to buy around 7-1/4 percent on the long bond," said Canning.
He expects the yield to continue edging up toward 7.6 percent by the end of the year as inflation data begin to deteriorate. "That would offer pretty good value for next year."
